solution.concept_anchor: Intra-British authority conflict over Treaty of Surat
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students associate Warren Hastings with aggressive British expansion and assume he would have endorsed Raghoba's cause, when in fact he actively repudiated the Bombay Council's unilateral action.
elimination_logic: Eliminate options linking the Bengal Council to the Treaty of Surat — the Treaty was signed unilaterally by the Bombay Council without Bengal's approval.
Eliminate any option suggesting Warren Hastings endorsed the Bombay Council's action — he repudiated it via the Treaty of Purandar.
The correct answer identifies the Bombay Presidency as acting unilaterally against the Bengal Council's authority, exposing intra-British governance conflict.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students familiar with Warren Hastings's general aggressiveness may assume he supported the Treaty of Surat. In reality, the Bombay Presidency acted unilaterally, and Hastings, as Governor-General, asserted Bengal's supremacy by attempting to nullify it. The trap exploits the conflation of British expansionism with institutional unity — in 1775, the British presidencies were not yet fully subordinated to Bengal.
solution.final_explanation:
The First Anglo-Maratha War exposed a fundamental structural flaw in early British Indian governance. The Bombay Presidency, acting without authorization from the Bengal Council, signed the Treaty of Surat (1775) with Raghunathrao (Raghoba), a claimant to the Peshwaship. Warren Hastings, as Governor-General, viewed this as an unauthorized overreach and responded by dispatching a Bengal mission that produced the Treaty of Purandar (1776) — an attempt to nullify Surat.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Hastings did not endorse the Bombay Council's action; he actively sought to reverse it through Purandar.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The Calcutta Council did not initiate the Surat treaty — the Bombay Presidency did so unilaterally.
• Option (c): Correct. The Bombay Presidency's unilateral alliance with Raghoba conflicted directly with the Bengal Council's authority, making this the defining intra-British tension of the First War.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Nana Phadnavis opposed the Treaty of Surat on behalf of the Pune Darbar — he was not a party within the British authority dispute.

Value Addition:
• The Regulating Act of 1773 had theoretically made the Bengal Council supreme, but enforcement remained weak in 1775.
• Raghoba's cause was used by Bombay to gain Salsette and Bassein — territorial ambition drove the alliance.
• This internal British conflict delayed effective war-making and contributed to the eventual humiliation at Wadgaon.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Purandar nullification of Surat by Bengal Council

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Surat (1775) was signed between the Bombay Council and Raghunathrao, granting the British possession of Salsette and Bassein.
statement_analysis.reason: The Treaty of Surat was precisely this agreement — the Bombay Presidency allied with Raghoba in exchange for Salsette and Bassein, which were the territorial gains that motivated British involvement in the succession dispute.

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Purandar (1776) was concluded by the Bengal Council and successfully neutralized the Treaty of Surat by persuading the Pune Darbar to accept a negotiated partition of territories.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Bengal Council did produce the Treaty of Purandar to override Surat, it failed in implementation — the Pune Darbar did not honor its terms, and active hostilities eventually resumed, culminating in Wadgaon (1779).

statement_analysis.statement: The contradiction between the Treaty of Surat and the Treaty of Purandar reflected structural weaknesses in British India's governance, where separate presidencies could pursue conflicting diplomatic objectives.
statement_analysis.reason: The fact that two British presidencies produced mutually contradictory treaties with opposing Maratha parties is the textbook example of governance fragmentation in pre-Pitt's India Act (1784) British India.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students who know Purandar was meant to nullify Surat may assume it succeeded, leading them to mark Statement 2 as correct and choose option (d) instead of recognizing Purandar's failure in implementation.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Salsette and Bassein were indeed ceded under Surat — this is correct.
Examine Statement 2 carefully: Purandar attempted to neutralize Surat but failed in practice — the Pune Darbar did not accept the settlement, making Statement 2 incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: The inter-presidency contradiction is historically validated — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a partial truth that is dangerous: the Bengal Council did produce Purandar with the intent to nullify Surat, and negotiations occurred. But the treaty failed in implementation — the Pune Darbar under Nana Phadnavis never genuinely accepted its terms. A student who knows the treaty existed but not its outcome will mark it correct, falling for the trap of confusing initiation with success.
solution.final_explanation:
The contrast between the treaties of Surat (1775) and Purandar (1776) encapsulates the governance crisis of early British India. The Bombay Presidency signed Surat unilaterally; Warren Hastings's Bengal Council responded with Purandar to reassert supremacy — but Purandar itself collapsed in implementation, leaving the conflict unresolved until Salbai (1782).

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Bombay Council ceded Salsette and Bassein to the British in exchange for military support for Raghoba — this is accurate.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Purandar failed in practice. The Pune Darbar under Nana Phadnavis did not honor it, and war eventually broke out, leading to Wadgaon (1779).
• Statement 3 — Correct: The mutual repudiation between two British presidencies is a classic instance of pre-Pitt's India Act governance failure.

Value Addition:
• Pitt's India Act (1784) was partly motivated by the chaos exposed during the First Anglo-Maratha War — it strengthened London's control over the presidencies.
• Salsette (near modern Mumbai) remained with the British even after Purandar's failure — a de facto gain despite treaty confusion.
• Nana Phadnavis's diplomatic skill in exploiting British disunity was crucial to Maratha survival during this period.

solution.concept_anchor: Convention of Wadgaon — British capitulation terms and ratification

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Convention of Wadgaon (1779), the Bombay army was required to restore all territories acquired since 1773 and to provide hostages as a guarantee of compliance.
statement_analysis.reason: These were indeed the humiliating terms — the British had to restore conquests since 1773 and surrender hostages, making Wadgaon the most severe formal British capitulation to an Indian power in this era.

statement_analysis.statement: Warren Hastings promptly ratified the Convention of Wadgaon, recognizing that the Bombay army's military situation left no alternative.
statement_analysis.reason: Hastings explicitly refused to ratify Wadgaon, declaring it unauthorized. He dispatched fresh forces from Bengal under Colonel Goddard to resume the campaign, effectively repudiating the convention.

statement_analysis.statement: The Convention of Wadgaon represents the only occasion during the three Anglo-Maratha Wars when British forces were compelled to formally agree to return previously acquired territories.
statement_analysis.reason: While Wadgaon was uniquely humiliating, characterizing it as the only such instance during all three wars requires excessive precision; more critically, Hastings's refusal to ratify meant the restoration never actually occurred — the statement misleadingly implies the terms were fully executed.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Statement 1 is accurate about the terms may mark only Statement 2 as incorrect and choose option (a), missing that Statement 3's claim about execution of terms is also problematic.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: The terms — restoration of conquests since 1773 and hostages — are historically accurate; Statement 1 is correct, not incorrect.
Check Statement 2: Hastings refused to ratify Wadgaon and dispatched Colonel Goddard — Statement 2 is factually wrong, so it qualifies as 'NOT correct'.

Examine Statement 3: The restoration of territories was never actually carried out since Hastings repudiated the convention — the statement implies execution of terms, making it misleading and NOT correct.
Both Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the obvious trap — students who know Hastings repudiated Wadgaon will quickly identify it as incorrect. Statement 3 is the subtle trap: it sounds like a reasonable historical claim, but it implies the terms of Wadgaon were actually implemented (the restoration happened), which they were not, since Hastings refused ratification. A well-prepared student must distinguish between terms agreed upon and terms executed.
solution.final_explanation:
The Convention of Wadgaon (1779) stands as the most dramatic British military setback during the Anglo-Maratha Wars. Colonel Cockburn's surrounded Bombay army was forced into a humiliating agreement by Maratha commanders.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The terms — restoring conquests since 1773 and providing hostages — are historically accurate and represent the depth of British humiliation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Warren Hastings vehemently refused to ratify Wadgaon, dispatching Colonel Goddard from Bengal to continue the campaign. This was a direct assertion of Bengal's authority over the Bombay Presidency.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Because Hastings repudiated the convention, the territorial restoration was never implemented. The statement's implication that the terms were executed is factually wrong.

Value Addition:
• Wadgaon is historically significant as the only formal capitulation document signed by a British army commander against an Indian power during this period.
• Nana Phadnavis and Mahadji Scindia were key architects of the Maratha strategy that produced Wadgaon.
• The episode accelerated British legislative reform — the Regulating Act's inadequacy in preventing such debacles strengthened the case for Pitt's India Act (1784).

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Salbai terms and Mahadji Scindia's mediation role

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Salbai (1782) included a provision for a 20-year peace between the British and the Maratha Confederacy.
statement_analysis.reason: The 20-year peace clause was a defining feature of Salbai, giving the British critical time to consolidate their position in the Deccan before the next major confrontation.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Treaty of Salbai, Raghunathrao (Raghoba) was recognized as the legitimate Peshwa by both parties.
statement_analysis.reason: Raghoba's cause was permanently abandoned — he was pensioned off, and the British recognized Madhavrao II (Sawai Madhavrao) as the Peshwa, the very position Raghoba had claimed.

statement_analysis.statement: Mahadji Scindia served as the principal mediator between the British and the Maratha Confederacy in the negotiations leading to the Treaty of Salbai.
statement_analysis.reason: Mahadji Scindia's role as mediator at Salbai was a landmark in his diplomatic career, establishing him as the most powerful and strategically indispensable Maratha chief of the era.

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Salbai restored to the British all territories they had lost under the Convention of Wadgaon (1779).
statement_analysis.reason: Salbai operated on a broad status quo principle — the British did not fully recover all Wadgaon losses. More precisely, Salsette was retained by the British, but the treaty was not a restoration of all Wadgaon-era losses; the status quo ante broadly applied.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as accurate may assume Statement 4 is also true (since Salbai 'restored British prestige'), landing on 'Only three' — but Statement 4 overstates what was actually recovered.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: The 20-year peace clause is a documented term of Salbai — correct.
Examine Statement 2: Raghoba was pensioned off, not recognized as Peshwa — Madhavrao II was recognized; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: Mahadji Scindia's mediation at Salbai is historically established — correct.
Examine Statement 4: Salbai was a status quo treaty; it did not restore all Wadgaon losses specifically — Statement 4 overstates the recovery; incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — answer is 'Only two', option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is the key trap. Since Salbai 'restored British prestige' after Wadgaon, students assume it also restored all Wadgaon territorial losses. In reality, Salbai was a status quo arrangement — the British retained Salsette but did not receive a comprehensive rollback of all Wadgaon terms. The narrative of 'British prestige restored' is conflated with 'territorial recovery', which is a classic partial-truth trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The Treaty of Salbai (1782) ended the First Anglo-Maratha War on terms that were diplomatically complex rather than a clear victory for either side. The 20-year peace gave the British breathing room, while Mahadji Scindia emerged as the indispensable power broker.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 20-year peace clause was central to Salbai's strategic value for the British.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Raghoba was pensioned off. The British recognition went to Madhavrao II, not Raghoba — abandoning the very pretext for British intervention.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Mahadji Scindia's mediation at Salbai was his diplomatic masterwork, elevating his stature enormously.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Salbai was a status quo treaty, not a comprehensive territorial restoration. The British retained Salsette but did not recover all Wadgaon-era losses specifically.

Value Addition:
• Salbai is sometimes described as a 'diplomatic draw' — neither side achieved its original war aims fully.
• Mahadji Scindia's mediation role gave him leverage over both the British and the Peshwa, which he used to extend Maratha power northward.
• The 20-year peace (1782–1803) maps almost exactly to the gap between the First and Second Anglo-Maratha Wars.

solution.concept_anchor: Governors-General matched to Anglo-Maratha Wars
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) incorrectly pairs Cornwallis with the Second War; students who know Cornwallis was active in India during this period and that he succeeded Wellesley may conflate recall-and-succession with presiding over the war.
elimination_logic: Anchor on the most unambiguous match: Lord Hastings and the Third War (1817–18) — this is fixed; eliminate options that misplace Hastings.
Confirm Warren Hastings with the First War (1775–82) — the Bombay vs. Bengal Council conflict was directly managed by him; eliminate options placing him elsewhere.
Lord Wellesley is associated with the Second War (1803–05) and the subsidiary alliance system — confirm this and eliminate option (a) which places Cornwallis instead.
The correct combination A-2, B-3, C-1 corresponds to option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap targets students who know that Cornwallis succeeded Lord Wellesley and confuse 'ending the war' with 'presiding over it'. Cornwallis was recalled to India after Wellesley precisely because Wellesley's wars were seen as overreach — Cornwallis came to wind down hostilities, not to conduct the Second War. Students may also confuse the two 'Hastings' — Warren Hastings (First War) and Lord Hastings (Third War) — and assign them to the wrong wars.
solution.final_explanation:
The three Anglo-Maratha Wars spanned nearly half a century and three distinct Governors-General, each with a different strategic temperament and outcome.

Correct pairings:
• A (Warren Hastings) → 2 (First Anglo-Maratha War, 1775–82): Hastings managed the crisis created by the Bombay Presidency's unilateral action, repudiated Wadgaon, and eventually oversaw the Treaty of Salbai.
• B (Lord Wellesley) → 3 (Second Anglo-Maratha War, 1803–05): Wellesley's subsidiary alliance strategy triggered the Second War; his generals Arthur Wellesley and Lake won decisive battles but Wellesley was recalled for overreach.
• C (Lord Hastings) → 1 (Third Anglo-Maratha War, 1817–18): Lord Hastings launched the encircling movement against Pindaris, which drew Maratha chiefs into open conflict, ending with the abolition of the Peshwaship.

The trap pairing is B-Cornwallis: Cornwallis did return to India after Wellesley, but only to reverse policies — he did not conduct the Second War.

Value Addition:
• 'Warren Hastings' and 'Lord Hastings' are two different persons — a classic UPSC naming trap.
• Wellesley was recalled in 1805; Cornwallis replaced him briefly but died shortly after arriving.
• Lord Hastings's Third War (1817–18) permanently ended Maratha political independence as a confederacy.

solution.concept_anchor: Nana Phadnavis — minister role and Maratha unity
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true may assume R explains A without scrutinizing whether the causal arrow runs from Nana's death to disunity (correct) or from his title to his effectiveness (what R actually claims).
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Nana Phadnavis died in 1800 and Maratha disunity did accelerate thereafter, directly contributing to Second War vulnerability. A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Nana Phadnavis held the position of Amatya (minister/administrator) in the Peshwa's court, not the Peshwaship itself. R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — R states his title (Amatya, not Peshwa), which is a fact about his institutional role. A states the consequence of his death on Maratha unity. His title does not causally explain why his death weakened Maratha unity — his diplomatic skill and personal authority do. R is an independent fact, not the causal explanation for A.

Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — correct option is (b)... Wait: re-reading — A says his death in 1800 weakened Maratha unity, R says he held the title Amatya not Peshwa. R does not causally explain A. Correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is reversed causation. A student might reason: 'Because he was Amatya (not Peshwa), his authority was personal rather than institutional, and so his death was irreplaceable — therefore R explains A.' This reasoning sounds plausible but it inserts a causal bridge that R itself does not contain. R is a statement of institutional title, not an explanation of why his death caused disunity. The actual reason for A is his personal diplomatic genius and coalition-building ability — which is not what R says.
solution.final_explanation:
Nana Phadnavis was arguably the most consequential Maratha statesman of the late 18th century. As Amatya (minister) under successive Peshwas, he was the de facto architect of Maratha diplomatic resistance during the First Anglo-Maratha War and the negotiations at Salbai.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: After Nana's death in 1800, Maratha unity collapsed rapidly. The internecine conflict between Baji Rao II, Holkar, and Scindia — which had been partially restrained by Nana's political management — spiraled out of control, directly enabling British exploitation via the Treaty of Bassein (1802).
• Reason (R) — Correct: Nana Phadnavis was indeed the Amatya (minister), not the Peshwa. This distinction is important — he exercised power through institutional influence and personal ability, not through the Peshwaship.
• Causal relationship — R does NOT explain A: R identifies his institutional title, which is a separate fact from why his death caused disunity. The explanation for A lies in his irreplaceable personal qualities and diplomatic network — not in his title.

Value Addition:
• 'Nana Phadnavis' is sometimes called 'the Maratha Machiavelli' for his diplomatic cunning.
• His full name was Balaji Janardan Bhanu; 'Nana' was a honorific and 'Phadnavis' referred to his administrative portfolio.
• His death in 1800 is considered a turning point — the Maratha Confederacy was never again able to present a unified front to the British.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence of key battles in Second Anglo-Maratha War 1803
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who associate Assaye with Arthur Wellesley's most celebrated victory may place it last as the 'climactic' battle, when in fact Assaye (September 1803) preceded both Argaon (November 1803) and Laswari (November 1803).
elimination_logic: Assaye was fought in September 1803 — it was the first of the three major battles; eliminate any option placing Assaye after Laswari or Argaon.
Laswari (November 1, 1803) and Argaon (November 29, 1803) were both fought in November — Laswari marginally preceded Argaon.
The correct sequence is Assaye → Laswari → Argaon, corresponding to option (b).
Eliminate option (a) which reverses Assaye and Laswari, and option (d) which places Argaon first.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is temporal — all three battles occurred in 1803, and students who cannot recall the precise months may guess based on dramatic significance rather than chronology. Assaye is the most famous battle (Wellesley called it his finest), leading students to assume it came last as the war's climax. In reality it came first, in September, followed by the November battles of Laswari (north) and Argaon (Deccan).
solution.final_explanation:
The Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) was fought on two fronts simultaneously — Arthur Wellesley commanded the Deccan theater while General Lake commanded operations in Hindustan.

Correct sequence: Assaye (September 23, 1803) → Laswari (November 1, 1803) → Argaon (November 29, 1803)

• Assaye: Fought first, in September 1803. Arthur Wellesley defeated the combined forces of Scindia and Bhonsle in a costly but decisive engagement. Wellesley later said it was the hardest battle he ever fought.
• Laswari: Fought on November 1, 1803, in Hindustan. General Lake defeated Scindia's regular infantry, securing British control over the Delhi-Agra region.
• Argaon: Fought on November 29, 1803, in the Deccan. Wellesley defeated Bhonsle's forces, leading directly to the Treaty of Deogaon.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a) — Laswari → Assaye → Argaon: Incorrect; Assaye was in September, Laswari in November.
• Option (c) — Argaon → Assaye → Laswari: Incorrect; Argaon was the last of the three.
• Option (d) — Argaon → Laswari → Assaye: Completely reversed.

Value Addition:
• Assaye is in present-day Maharashtra; Laswari is in Rajasthan.
• Both Deogaon (after Argaon) and Surji-Anjangaon (after Assaye) were concluded in December 1803.
• The two-front strategy was Lord Wellesley's key innovation in fighting the Maratha Confederacy.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Bassein — subsidiary alliance applied to Peshwa as confederacy head
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may select the 'divide and rule' explanation because the British clearly exploited Maratha rivalry, but the specific mechanism in the scenario is the subsidiary alliance system — Baji Rao II's formal surrender of foreign policy autonomy — not a general divide-and-rule tactic.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a ruler who accepts British troops on his territory and surrenders the right to conduct independent diplomacy — this is the definitional core of the subsidiary alliance system.
Eliminate option (a): 'Ring-fence policy' refers to a defensive perimeter concept, not a formal treaty requiring stationing of troops and foreign policy surrender.
Eliminate option (b): Divide-and-rule is a general strategy, not the specific legal-constitutional mechanism that made Bassein historically decisive.
Eliminate option (c): Doctrine of Lapse applies to inheritance and annexation after 1848 under Dalhousie — anachronistic for 1802.
The mechanism is the subsidiary alliance system — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario deliberately includes the phrase 'playing Maratha chiefs against each other' to plant the divide-and-rule option as an appealing answer. But the question asks which specific British policy instrument was formalized — and the answer is the subsidiary alliance. The conflation trap merges the strategic context (exploiting Maratha rivalry) with the specific policy tool (subsidiary alliance), which are distinct concepts.
solution.final_explanation:
The subsidiary alliance system, developed and systematically applied by Lord Wellesley, was the most consequential British policy instrument for establishing paramountcy over Indian states in the early 19th century.

Core elements: (1) British troops stationed permanently in the ruler's territory; (2) the ruler surrenders authority to conduct independent foreign relations; (3) the ruler cedes territories (or pays cash) for the maintenance of these troops; (4) in return, the British guarantee protection from external threats.

Application to the scenario: The ruler (Baji Rao II) accepted British troops at Pune, surrendered diplomatic autonomy, and ceded territories — precisely the three definitional elements of the subsidiary alliance. This is what the Treaty of Bassein (1802) formalized.

• Option (a) — Ring-fence policy: Lord Hastings's strategy of encircling Pindaris; a military containment concept, not a treaty-based subordination mechanism.
• Option (b) — Divide and rule: A general imperial strategy, not the specific institutional arrangement described.
• Option (c) — Doctrine of Lapse: Dalhousie's post-1848 annexation tool based on inheritance — wrong era entirely.
• Option (d) — Subsidiary alliance: Correct; matches all three definitional elements in the scenario.

Value Addition:
• Bassein was called a 'death warrant of Maratha independence' because as head of the Confederacy, the Peshwa's submission implied subordination of all Maratha chiefs.
• Hyderabad (1798) and Mysore (1799) were the earliest applications of the subsidiary alliance before the Marathas.
• Scindia and Bhonsle refused to recognize Bassein — this refusal was the proximate cause of the Second War.

solution.concept_anchor: Cuttack ceded by Bhonsle not Scindia — territorial attribution
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Delhi and Agra were ceded under Surji-Anjangaon (Scindia's treaty) may assume all northern territorial cessions belonged to Scindia, leading them to incorrectly exclude Ahmadnagar rather than Cuttack.
elimination_logic: Identify which territories were ceded under the Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (Scindia's treaty): Delhi, Agra, Broach, Ahmadnagar — all in north and west India.
Cuttack (in Odisha) was ceded under the Treaty of Deogaon by Bhonsle, not Scindia — it is geographically and treaty-wise distinct.
Delhi, Agra, and Broach all belong to Scindia's cessions under Surji-Anjangaon — they share a common treaty origin.
Cuttack does not belong to this group — it is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap exploits the fact that students learning about British gains in the Second War often memorize them as a combined list without noting which chief ceded which territory. Cuttack is far to the east, ceded by Bhonsle under Deogaon — but students who don't track the treaty-chief-territory connection will struggle to separate it from Scindia's cessions. Ahmadnagar (option c) sounds potentially odd because it is in the Deccan, but it was specifically ceded by Scindia under Surji-Anjangaon.
solution.final_explanation:
The Second Anglo-Maratha War produced multiple treaties with different Maratha chiefs, and a precise knowledge of which chief ceded which territory is essential.

• Option (a) — Delhi: Ceded by Scindia under the Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (1803). Belongs to the group.
• Option (b) — Cuttack: Ceded by Bhonsle of Nagpur under the Treaty of Deogaon (1803). This is the odd one out — it belongs to a different treaty and a different Maratha chief.
• Option (c) — Ahmadnagar: Ceded by Scindia under Surji-Anjangaon. Belongs to the same treaty as Delhi and Agra.
• Option (d) — Broach: Also ceded by Scindia under Surji-Anjangaon. Belongs to the group.

Value Addition:
• Cuttack's cession gave the British control over the eastern coastline from Bengal to Madras — strategically immense.
• Surji-Anjangaon made the British the effective protectors of the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II.
• The Treaty of Deogaon (with Bhonsle) was signed on December 17, 1803; Surji-Anjangaon (with Scindia) on December 30, 1803.

solution.concept_anchor: Mughal Emperor's status after 1803 — protection vs. pensioner

statement_analysis.statement: Following the Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (1803), the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II came under British 'protection', with the British replacing the Marathas as the power controlling his court at Delhi.
statement_analysis.reason: The treaty transferred the role of de facto protector of the Mughal court from Scindia to the British — Shah Alam II was blind and politically powerless, but the British now controlled access to Mughal symbolic authority.

statement_analysis.statement: As a consequence of the 1803 treaty arrangements, the Mughal Emperor ceased to be a nominally sovereign ruler and formally became a British pensioner with no remaining imperial title.
statement_analysis.reason: The Mughal Emperor retained his nominal imperial title until 1857 — the 1803 arrangements did not abolish his sovereignty on paper. He became a British pensioner and lost his title only after the suppression of the 1857 uprising, when Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who conflate 'British protection' with 'end of Mughal sovereignty' will mark both statements as correct, choosing option (a) without distinguishing between nominal imperial status and actual powerlessness.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Surji-Anjangaon transferred Scindia's protectorate role over Delhi and the Mughal court to the British — Statement 1 is correct.

Examine Statement 2: The Mughal Emperor retained his nominal title until 1857 — it was only after Bahadur Shah Zafar's trial and exile following the 1857 uprising that the title was formally abolished. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Correct answer: Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is a scope-extension: 'no remaining imperial title' goes too far. Students who know the Mughals became powerless and dependent on British support after 1803 may assume this meant formal abolition of the title. In reality, the Emperor retained the nominal title of Mughal Emperor until 1857. The British maintained this fiction because the symbolic legitimacy of the Mughal name was politically useful to them — a pensioner emperor posed no threat and provided useful ceremonial cover.
solution.final_explanation:
The year 1803 was transformative for the Mughal dynasty. With Scindia's defeat and the Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon, British forces entered Delhi and the Mughal Emperor transitioned from Maratha protection to British protection.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The British replaced the Marathas as the controlling power at Delhi. Shah Alam II, already blind and militarily impotent, now received a British pension and British military protection instead of Maratha support.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This overstates the 1803 change. The Mughal Emperor continued to hold his nominal imperial title — even issuing firmans (imperial orders) in his name. This nominal sovereignty lasted until 1857, when Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried for treason and exiled to Rangoon after the uprising failed.

Value Addition:
• The British deliberately preserved the Mughal title after 1803 because it gave their own authority a veneer of traditional legitimacy.
• Shah Alam II had been blinded by Ghulam Qadir (Afghan chief) in 1788 — long before the British arrived.
• The connection between 1803 and 1857: the pensioner emperor at Delhi became the rallying symbol for the 1857 uprising, ultimately costing the last Mughal his title.

solution.concept_anchor: Pindaris — identity and connection to Maratha chiefs
solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Rohilla mercenaries' sounds plausible as a category of irregular fighters in 18th-century India; students unfamiliar with the precise definition of Pindaris may confuse them with other known irregular groups like Rohillas or Afghans.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): Thuggee practitioners operated in a completely different mode — ritual stranglers targeting travelers, suppressed in the 1830s under Sleeman; not cavalry plunderers attached to Maratha armies.
Eliminate option (c): Rohilla mercenaries were a specific Afghan-origin group in Rohilkhand; they were not the groups attached to Maratha armies as camp followers and plunderers.
Eliminate option (d): Bargirs were Maratha cavalry soldiers who used state-supplied horses — a defined military category, not irregular plunderers.
Pindaris were irregular horsemen attached informally to Maratha armies, recruited from diverse communities, who sustained themselves through organized plunder — option (a) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is plausible-fabrication via category confusion. 'Rohilla mercenaries' (option c) and 'Bargirs' (option d) are real historical categories from the same broad era, making them plausible distractors for students who know the period generally but cannot precisely define Pindaris. The Thuggee option is a classic era-conflation trap — both Pindari suppression and Thuggee suppression were British internal security operations, but they occurred two decades apart and involved completely different groups.
solution.final_explanation:
Pindaris were one of the most distinctive features of the military landscape of late Maratha India.

• Option (a) — Correct: Pindaris were irregular horsemen recruited from diverse communities — neither a single caste nor a tribe — who attached themselves to Maratha armies and sustained themselves through systematic plunder of civilian areas. They were not formally part of any Maratha chief's official forces but received informal patronage.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Thuggee practitioners were ritual criminals who strangled travelers — a completely different phenomenon suppressed in the 1830s by William Sleeman under Lord Bentinck.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Rohilla mercenaries were Afghan-origin fighters based in Rohilkhand; while they were irregular in some contexts, they are a distinct historical group unconnected to Pindari activities.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Bargirs were Maratha cavalrymen who used state-supplied horses — a defined military category within the formal Maratha military structure.

Value Addition:
• The three principal Pindari leaders were Chitu, Wasil Muhammad, and Karim Khan.
• Scindia and Holkar's informal protection of Pindaris became the British pretext for demanding they disown them — the Treaty of Gwalior (1817) with Scindia was specifically for this purpose.
• Pindari raids extended into British-controlled territories in Bengal, Madras, and Bombay, generating civilian complaints that Lord Hastings used to justify military action.

solution.concept_anchor: Battle-to-Maratha chief matching in Third Anglo-Maratha War
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) assigns Sitabaldi to Holkar, which is a plausible error: students who associate 'Nagpur' with Holkar (because both are in the Deccan region) may make this swap, when in fact Sitabaldi was Bhonsle's battle.
elimination_logic: Anchor on the most textbook fact: Battle of Khadki (1817) involved Baji Rao II attacking the British Residency at Pune — this is fixed; it pairs with the Peshwa.
Sitabaldi (1817) was fought at Nagpur, which is the seat of the Bhonsle chief — pair Sitabaldi with Bhonsle.
Mahidpur (1817) was the decisive defeat of Holkar by John Malcolm — pair Mahidpur with Holkar.
The correct combination A-2, B-3, C-1 corresponds to option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits the geographic proximity of Nagpur and Holkar's territories in student memory. Holkar's base was Indore (in present Madhya Pradesh), while Bhonsle's base was Nagpur (in present Maharashtra). Sitabaldi is near Nagpur — therefore it was Bhonsle's battle. Students who conflate the two Deccan chiefs will swap Sitabaldi and Mahidpur across the chiefs, choosing option (b). Mahidpur is in Madhya Pradesh — closer to Holkar's territory — which is the correct pairing.
solution.final_explanation:
The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–18) involved three distinct Maratha powers, each defeated in a separate engagement.

Correct pairings:
• A (Battle of Khadki, 1817) → 2 (Peshwa Baji Rao II): Baji Rao II launched a surprise attack on the British Residency at Pune, triggering open war. He was ultimately defeated and the Peshwaship was abolished.
• B (Battle of Sitabaldi, 1817) → 3 (Bhonsle of Nagpur): Bhonsle's forces attacked the British cantonment near Nagpur. The British garrison held out and Bhonsle was defeated, leading to Nagpur's subordination.
• C (Battle of Mahidpur, 1817) → 1 (Holkar of Indore): John Malcolm decisively defeated Holkar's forces at Mahidpur on the Sipra River, leading to the Treaty of Mandasor (1818).

Key trap: Sitabaldi is near Nagpur (Bhonsle's seat), not Holkar's territory — this geographic anchor resolves the confusion.

Value Addition:
• The Battle of Mahidpur was fought on December 21, 1817 — Malcolm's victory was rapid and decisive.
• After Sitabaldi, Bhonsle's Nagpur became a dependent state under a Resident.
• The Third War was completed within a year (1817–18), reflecting British military superiority and Maratha disunity.

solution.concept_anchor: Baji Rao II pensioned at Bithur — last Peshwa's fate
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Baji Rao II was pensioned off near Kanpur may confuse Bithur with Kanpur itself, choosing the Kanpur pairing as correctly matched.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Baji Rao II was pensioned off at Bithur — a town near Kanpur — not at Kanpur itself. The pair 'Baji Rao II — Kanpur' is incorrectly matched.
Eliminate option (b): The Peshwaship was abolished in 1818, not 1817. The year 1817 was when Khadki was fought, but the formal abolition came after Baji Rao II's surrender in 1818.
Eliminate option (d): The Treaty of Mandasor (1818) was concluded with Holkar of Indore, not with Bhonsle of Nagpur. Bhonsle's settlement was the Treaty with Bhonsle/Nagpur.
Option (c) — Baji Rao II pensioned at Bithur — is correctly matched; Bithur is the precise location.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap works on two levels: Bithur vs. Kanpur (both in UP, very close together) and Holkar vs. Bhonsle for the Treaty of Mandasor. Students who remember 'Baji Rao II was sent somewhere near Kanpur' will choose Kanpur instead of Bithur. The Bithur connection is historically critical because Nana Saheb — Baji Rao II's adopted son who lived at Bithur — became a leader of the 1857 uprising, making this a cross-topic UPSC linkage question.
solution.final_explanation:
The end of the Third Anglo-Maratha War brought a permanent end to Maratha political power. Each pairing must be verified precisely.

• Option (a) — Baji Rao II : Kanpur: Incorrectly matched. He was pensioned off at Bithur, a town approximately 20 km from Kanpur, not at Kanpur itself.
• Option (b) — Abolition of Peshwaship : 1817: Incorrectly matched. The Peshwaship was formally abolished in 1818 after Baji Rao II's surrender, not 1817 (when Khadki was fought).
• Option (c) — Baji Rao II : Bithur: Correctly matched. After surrendering, Baji Rao II was granted a pension and allowed to live out his days at Bithur near Kanpur.
• Option (d) — Treaty of Mandasor : Bhonsle of Nagpur: Incorrectly matched. Mandasor was concluded with Holkar of Indore; Bhonsle's terms were separate.

Value Addition:
• Nana Saheb, Baji Rao II's adopted son at Bithur, became one of the prominent leaders of the 1857 uprising — a direct cross-topic connection.
• The abolition of the Peshwaship meant the British annexed Pune and the Peshwa's territories, which were eventually merged into the Bombay Presidency.
• Baji Rao II died at Bithur in 1851, six years before the uprising in which his adopted son played a key role.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequential acceptance of subsidiary alliance by Maratha chiefs
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Scindia was the most powerful Maratha chief and therefore assume he was brought in first may choose option (c), which places Scindia before the Peshwa.
elimination_logic: Anchor on the Treaty of Bassein (1802) — the Peshwa was the first Maratha chief to accept the subsidiary alliance; this is fixed.

After the Second War, Bhonsle accepted under Treaty of Deogaon (December 1803) and Scindia under Surji-Anjangaon (December 1803) — Deogaon was signed slightly earlier (December 17) vs. Surji-Anjangaon (December 30).
Holkar was the last and most resistant — he was partially incorporated only under the Treaty of Rajpurghat (1806).
Correct sequence: Peshwa (1802) → Bhonsle (December 1803) → Scindia (December 1803) → Holkar (1806) — the answer placing Peshwa first and Holkar last is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap operates at two levels. First, students may assume that the most powerful chief (Scindia) was dealt with first — in reality, the Peshwa as formal head of the Confederacy was the first to accept, specifically because his political weakness made him most susceptible. Second, Bhonsle and Scindia accepted within the same month (December 1803), but Deogaon slightly preceded Surji-Anjangaon, creating a fine-grained sequencing challenge.
solution.final_explanation:
The subsidiary alliance was not applied simultaneously to all Maratha chiefs — it was a sequential process that unfolded over four years.

Correct sequence:
1. Peshwa Baji Rao II (Treaty of Bassein, December 1802): First and most consequential acceptance — as Confederacy head, this had implications for all chiefs.
2. Bhonsle of Nagpur (Treaty of Deogaon, December 17, 1803): Defeated by Arthur Wellesley at Argaon; ceded Cuttack and part of Berar.
3. Scindia (Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon, December 30, 1803): Defeated at Assaye and Laswari; ceded Delhi, Agra, Broach, Ahmadnagar.
4. Holkar (Treaty of Rajpurghat, 1806): The most resistant; retained most territories and was only partially incorporated, benefiting from Wellesley's recall.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a) places Scindia before Peshwa — incorrect; Peshwa came first in 1802.
• Option (c) places Holkar before Bhonsle — incorrect; Holkar was the most resistant and came last.
• Option (d) places Bhonsle first — incorrect; the Peshwa was first.

Value Addition:
• Gaikwad of Baroda had already accepted a subsidiary-style arrangement earlier and was not a major actor in the Second War.
• Holkar's relatively favorable outcome under Rajpurghat was partly due to the British change of policy after Wellesley's recall.
• The sequential nature of subsidiary alliance imposition was central to British strategy — divide each chief from the others.

solution.concept_anchor: Holkar's guerrilla resistance and British setbacks 1804–1805

statement_analysis.statement: Yashwantrao Holkar's military strategy during 1804–05 relied primarily on guerrilla tactics and mobility rather than set-piece battles, which limited the effectiveness of British conventional military pursuit.
statement_analysis.reason: Holkar's guerrilla approach — rapid movement, avoiding pitched battles, stretching British supply lines — was precisely why General Lake's pursuit proved frustrating and ultimately inconclusive.

statement_analysis.statement: The British siege of Bharatpur (1805) failed against the Jat ruler Ranjit Singh Gujar, representing a rare setback that contributed to reassessing the pace of British military expansion.
statement_analysis.reason: The Bharatpur siege was a notable British failure — the Jat fortifications proved resistant and the British suffered heavy casualties, contributing to the political climate that facilitated Wellesley's recall.

statement_analysis.statement: The recall of Lord Wellesley and the subsequent policy shift under Lord Cornwallis resulted in a comprehensive treaty that fully subordinated Holkar under the subsidiary alliance on British terms.
statement_analysis.reason: The Treaty of Rajpurghat (1806) with Holkar was notably more favorable to Holkar than British terms offered during Wellesley's tenure — Holkar retained most of his territories. It was not 'comprehensive subordination on British terms' but a relative concession resulting from policy reversal.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the Holkar phase ended in a treaty and that Cornwallis replaced Wellesley may assume the final settlement was favorable to the British and mark Statement 3 as correct, choosing option (c) instead of (a).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Holkar's guerrilla strategy is historically documented and explains Lake's difficulty — correct.
Verify Statement 2: The Bharatpur siege failure is an established fact — British forces under Lake failed to take the fort — correct.
Examine Statement 3: Rajpurghat was relatively favorable to Holkar — Cornwallis's policy reversal softened British demands; 'full subordination on British terms' overstates the outcome — incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Statement 3 is incorrect — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the partial truth that Cornwallis did arrive and a treaty was signed. Students who correctly recall that Cornwallis replaced Wellesley and a settlement was reached may assume the British achieved their full objectives. The trap is in 'comprehensive subordination on British terms' — the Rajpurghat terms were actually a British concession, not a British victory. Holkar retained significant territory precisely because Wellesley's aggressive policy was reversed.
solution.final_explanation:
The Holkar phase (1804–05) of the Second Anglo-Maratha War revealed important limits of British military strategy and political will.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Holkar's mobile guerrilla warfare frustrated Lake's pursuit across a vast theater. This demonstrated that the British, while superior in set-piece engagements, struggled against fast-moving irregular forces.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Bharatpur siege (1805) was a genuine British failure. The Jat ruler Ranjit Singh Gujar's defenses — including mud fortifications that absorbed cannon fire — repelled multiple British assaults, causing significant casualties and embarrassment.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Treaty of Rajpurghat (1806) was a softer settlement than Wellesley had sought. Holkar retained most of his territories — the treaty reflected British political retreat under Cornwallis rather than military triumph.

Value Addition:
• Cornwallis died shortly after arriving in India in October 1805, having barely begun to implement the policy reversal.
• Bharatpur's success in 1805 was later reversed when the British captured the fort in 1826 under Lord Combermere.
• Holkar's relative success in 1806 made him the only Maratha chief who did not lose major territory in the Second War.

solution.concept_anchor: Pindaris — identity distinct from Thuggee and connection to Maratha armies

statement_analysis.statement: The Pindaris were irregular horsemen who sustained themselves through organized plunder and were informally attached to Maratha armies, deriving patronage from chiefs like Scindia and Holkar.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the accurate description — Pindaris were irregular, multi-community horsemen who received informal Maratha patronage and sustained themselves through raids, not a caste or tribe.

statement_analysis.statement: The Pindari suppression campaign of 1817 was part of the same historical phenomenon as the Thuggee suppression of the 1830s — both targeted organized criminal networks operating under the patronage of Indian princes.
statement_analysis.reason: Pindaris and Thuggee were entirely distinct phenomena: Pindaris were cavalry raiders attached to Maratha armies, suppressed in 1817–18 as part of the Third Anglo-Maratha War context; Thuggees were ritual stranglers targeting individual travelers, suppressed in the 1830s under William Sleeman — different era, different method, different British response.

statement_analysis.statement: Lord Hastings's 'Encircling Movement' against the Pindaris was specifically designed to avoid military confrontation with Maratha chiefs, targeting only the Pindari bands themselves.
statement_analysis.reason: The encircling movement inevitably targeted Maratha chiefs because Pindaris operated under their informal protection — the Treaty of Gwalior (1817) demanding Scindia disown Pindaris shows that the campaign was inseparable from confronting the chiefs themselves.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Statement 1 is accurate may stop there and choose option (a) assuming only Statement 2 is incorrect, missing that Statement 3 is also factually wrong.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Accurate description of Pindaris — irregular multi-community horsemen with Maratha patronage — this is NOT incorrect; exclude it.
Evaluate Statement 2: Conflates Pindari suppression with Thuggee suppression — two distinct phenomena separated by two decades — Statement 2 IS incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 3: The encircling movement did target Maratha chiefs (Treaty of Gwalior, Khadki, etc.) — the claim that it 'specifically avoided' Maratha chiefs is historically wrong — Statement 3 IS incorrect.
Both Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 employs a conflation trap — both Pindari and Thuggee suppression are 'British campaigns against Indian criminal networks under princely patronage', and students who remember both may conflate them into one continuous phenomenon. The key distinction is era (1817 vs. 1830s), method (cavalry raids vs. ritual strangulation), and British response mechanism (military campaign integrated with Anglo-Maratha War vs. civilian police operation under Sleeman). Statement 3 is subtler — it sounds reasonable to say 'Hastings targeted only Pindaris, not chiefs' but the historical record shows the campaign was inextricably linked to Maratha confrontation.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding what Pindaris were — and what they were not — is essential for correctly contextualizing the Third Anglo-Maratha War.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Pindaris were informal irregular horsemen drawn from diverse communities, attached to Maratha armies, sustained by plunder. They had no single caste or tribal identity.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The conflation of Pindaris with Thuggee is the classic exam trap. Thuggee involved ritual strangulation of travelers by organized gangs and was suppressed in the 1830s by Sleeman under Lord Bentinck — a completely different era, method, and administrative response.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Hastings's encircling movement could not separate Pindari suppression from Maratha confrontation because Pindaris operated under Maratha protection. The Treaty of Gwalior (1817) — requiring Scindia to formally disown Pindaris — shows how entwined the two campaigns were.

Value Addition:
• The three principal Pindari chiefs were Chitu, Wasil Muhammad, and Karim Khan — none survived or flourished post-1818.
• Chitu escaped into a jungle and was reportedly killed by a tiger — an unusual end for a feared raider.
• Pindari raids penetrated into Madras and Bengal, creating widespread civilian distress that gave Hastings the political justification to act.

statement_analysis.reason: Arthur Wellesley commanded the Deccan front, and Assaye was his most famous engagement — against the combined armies of Scindia and Bhonsle, whom he described as the hardest battle he ever fought.

statement_analysis.reason: Lake commanded the Hindustan front; Laswari was his decisive engagement against Scindia's northern forces, and its result — combined with the subsequent treaty — transferred Delhi and Agra to British control.

statement_analysis.reason: Argaon was fought by Arthur Wellesley in the Deccan theater against Bhonsle's forces — not by Lake, and not against Holkar. Lake operated in Hindustan, Wellesley in the Deccan.

statement_analysis.statement: Lord Wellesley's two-front strategy in the Second Anglo-Maratha War was unprecedented in British Indian military history up to that point in that it simultaneously engaged two major Maratha powers in geographically separated theaters.
statement_analysis.reason: The simultaneous two-front campaign against Scindia/Bhonsle in the Deccan and Scindia's northern forces in Hindustan was a strategically innovative deployment for British India at that time.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who find three correct statements may assume all four are correct and choose option (d), without catching that Statement 3 wrongly assigns Argaon to Lake against Holkar instead of Wellesley against Bhonsle.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Arthur Wellesley at Assaye in the Deccan — historically accurate and well-documented; correct.
Verify Statement 2: Lake at Laswari in the north, securing Delhi — correct.
Scrutinize Statement 3: Argaon was Wellesley vs. Bhonsle in the Deccan, not Lake vs. Holkar — this is a double entity-swap (wrong general, wrong opponent, wrong theater); incorrect.
Verify Statement 4: Simultaneous two-front strategy was indeed a strategic innovation — correct.
Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct — answer is 'Only three', option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a double entity-swap trap: it assigns the wrong general (Lake instead of Wellesley), the wrong opponent (Holkar instead of Bhonsle), and the wrong theater (Hindustan instead of Deccan) — all in one statement. Each error individually might be caught by a careful student, but combined they create a plausible-sounding claim about a real battle. Students who know Argaon was a real battle in the Second War but cannot recall the precise general-opponent pairing will mark it correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The Second Anglo-Maratha War's two-theater structure is a critical UPSC topic — matching generals to battles and theaters is a standard format.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Arthur Wellesley commanded the Deccan front. Assaye (September 1803) against Scindia-Bhonsle combined forces was the war's most famous engagement.
• Statement 2 — Correct: General Lake's Hindustan campaign included Laswari (November 1, 1803), which defeated Scindia's northern forces and opened Delhi to British control.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Argaon was fought in the Deccan by Arthur Wellesley against Bhonsle's forces (November 29, 1803). Lake did not fight at Argaon, and Holkar was not involved — he was a separate theater entirely.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The simultaneous two-front campaign was Lord Wellesley's strategic design — an unprecedented coordination for British India.

Value Addition:
• Arthur Wellesley later became the Duke of Wellington, famous for defeating Napoleon at Waterloo (1815).
• Laswari gave the British control over the Doab region and symbolic control of the former Mughal heartland.
• The two-front strategy prevented Maratha chiefs from reinforcing each other — a deliberate divide-and-destroy approach.

solution.concept_anchor: Maratha Confederacy fragmentation enabling British divide-and-rule
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true and note that Maratha disunity did help British strategy may quickly choose (a) without carefully examining whether the specific causal mechanism R describes actually explains A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — The British fought each Maratha chief separately in all three Anglo-Maratha Wars rather than confronting a unified Maratha force. A is factually correct.

Step 2: Is R correct? — The Maratha Confederacy comprised five principal houses (Peshwa, Scindia, Holkar, Bhonsle, Gaikwad) who maintained mutual rivalries and never achieved military unification against the British. R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — R directly explains A: because the five houses maintained mutual rivalries and failed to unify (R), the British were able to engage them individually rather than as a combined force (A). The causal link from R to A is direct and logical.
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A — correct option is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The structural fragmentation of the Maratha Confederacy is the most important systemic explanation for British success across all three Anglo-Maratha Wars.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: The British consistently pursued a strategy of engaging each Maratha chief separately. In the Second War, they fought Scindia and Bhonsle simultaneously but avoided provoking Holkar; then fought Holkar separately. In the Third War, they extracted a treaty from Scindia (Gwalior, 1817) before engaging the Peshwa and others.
• Reason (R) — Correct: The five principal houses — Peshwa, Scindia, Holkar, Bhonsle, and Gaikwad — had competing territorial ambitions. Their rivalries (e.g., Holkar vs. Peshwa in 1802, Scindia vs. Holkar throughout) prevented military coordination.
• Causal relationship — R explains A: The mutual rivalry among the five houses (R) is precisely what enabled the British strategy of fighting each separately (A). Without this fragmentation, a unified Maratha force could have presented far greater resistance.

Value Addition:
• Shivaji's original Maratha empire was centralized — the confederacy structure emerged gradually after his death and the weakening of the Peshwa system.
• The only moment of near-unity — the Maratha coalition at Panipat (1761) against Ahmad Shah Abdali — ended in catastrophic defeat.
• Even during the First War, Holkar and Scindia had competing interests that Nana Phadnavis had to manage carefully.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Bassein — signed with Peshwa as Confederacy head, not individual chief
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Bassein involved the Peshwa may choose option (a) because it correctly identifies the Peshwa, but option (a) adds 'on behalf of all Maratha chiefs who had collectively ratified it' — this is factually wrong; the chiefs did not collectively ratify it, and Scindia and Bhonsle explicitly rejected it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Treaty of Bassein was not collectively ratified by all Maratha chiefs — Scindia and Bhonsle specifically refused to recognize it.
Eliminate option (b): Bassein was signed by the Peshwa, not by Scindia — this is a direct entity-swap.
Eliminate option (d): Bassein was signed in 1802, not 1803; and it was signed with the Peshwa, not Holkar.
Option (c) correctly identifies Bassein as signed with the Peshwa as formal head of the Confederacy — whose acceptance had confederacy-wide implications even though other chiefs rejected it.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in option (a) is subtle: the Peshwa was indeed the signatory, which makes the first part of option (a) correct — but 'collectively ratified by all Maratha chiefs' extends the claim beyond historical reality. Scindia and Bhonsle's refusal to recognize Bassein was precisely what triggered the Second War. A student who reads quickly and recognizes 'Peshwa' as the correct party may select (a) without noticing the false collective ratification claim.
solution.final_explanation:
The Treaty of Bassein (December 31, 1802) is one of the most consequential diplomatic documents in the history of British India.

• Option (a): Incorrect. While the Peshwa was the signatory, the treaty was emphatically not collectively ratified by all Maratha chiefs. Scindia and Bhonsle rejected it as an unacceptable surrender — their opposition was the direct cause of the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Scindia did not sign Bassein. He was among the most vocal opponents of it. Scindia only formally accepted a subsidiary alliance later under Surji-Anjangaon (December 1803).
• Option (c): Correct. Bassein was signed with Peshwa Baji Rao II. As the formal head of the Maratha Confederacy, his acceptance carried symbolic confederacy-wide implications — which is precisely why historians called it a 'death warrant of Maratha independence'.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The year was 1802, not 1803; Holkar was not a signatory — he had actually defeated Baji Rao II, which drove the Peshwa into British arms.

Value Addition:
• The Treaty of Bassein was signed at Bassein (present-day Vasai, near Mumbai).
• Baji Rao II's flight to British protection after defeat by Holkar at Khadki/Poona (1802) was the immediate context.
• Bassein is sometimes compared to Allahabad Treaty (1765) in significance — both dramatically altered the balance of power in India.

statement_analysis.statement: Mahadji Scindia was recognized as the 'Deputy Regent of the Mughal Empire' (Vakil-i-Mutlaq) by Shah Alam II, giving him formal authority over the Mughal Emperor's affairs and making him the most powerful political figure in north India in the 1780s.
statement_analysis.reason: Shah Alam II did confer the title of Vakil-i-Mutlaq on Mahadji Scindia, recognizing his de facto control over the Mughal court at Delhi — making Scindia simultaneously a Maratha chief and the dominant power in the Mughal system.

statement_analysis.statement: Mahadji Scindia's death in 1803 directly preceded the Second Anglo-Maratha War, and the war's outbreak is primarily attributed to the power vacuum created by his passing.
statement_analysis.reason: Mahadji Scindia died in 1794, not 1803. The Second War began in 1803 — nine years after his death. While his death did contribute to Maratha disunity, attributing the Second War 'primarily' to his death is historically overstated; the Treaty of Bassein (1802) and Holkar-Peshwa rivalry were the proximate causes.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Mahadji was indeed dominant in north India and that his death weakened the Marathas may accept both statements as broadly true, choosing option (a) without catching the wrong year (1803 instead of 1794) in Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Mahadji Scindia held the title Vakil-i-Mutlaq from Shah Alam II in the 1780s — historically documented; correct.
Check the year in Statement 2: Mahadji Scindia died in 1794, not 1803 — this is a direct temporal error; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Even setting aside the year error: attributing the Second War 'primarily' to his death overstates the causal link — the Treaty of Bassein was the proximate cause.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a subtle temporal-swap: it says Scindia died in 1803, when he actually died in 1794. Students who remember that his death preceded the Second War and weakened the Marathas may not catch the nine-year discrepancy, especially under exam pressure. The causal logic in Statement 2 (death → Second War) is also exaggerated, but the year error is the clearest indicator of incorrectness.
solution.final_explanation:
Mahadji Scindia was one of the most consequential Indian political figures of the late 18th century, simultaneously a Maratha chief, de facto Mughal regent, and British interlocutor.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Shah Alam II conferred the title Vakil-i-Mutlaq (Regent of the Empire) on Mahadji Scindia, recognizing his control over Delhi. This dual authority — as both Maratha leader and Mughal regent — made him the dominant force in north India in the 1780s–90s.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Mahadji Scindia died in February 1794 at Wanowrie near Pune — not in 1803. The Second Anglo-Maratha War began in 1803, nine years later. His death did contribute to Maratha fragmentation, but the 'primarily' attribution is exaggerated, and the year is simply wrong.

Value Addition:
• Mahadji Scindia rebuilt the Maratha military using European-trained infantry under Benoit de Boigne — a significant modernization effort.
• After his death, his grandnephew Daulat Rao Scindia inherited power but lacked Mahadji's diplomatic skill.
• Daulat Rao Scindia's confrontation with the British in 1803 (Second War) ended in the loss of Delhi and Agra — territories Mahadji had painstakingly accumulated.

solution.concept_anchor: Nana Phadnavis — title Amatya, not Peshwa
solution.strong_distractor: a — 'Peshwa' is the most famous Maratha title and students who know Nana Phadnavis was the most powerful figure in Pune may assume he held the Peshwaship, when in fact the Peshwa was the nominal head while Nana exercised power as Amatya.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Nana Phadnavis was never the Peshwa — he was a minister who wielded power behind successive Peshwas; the Peshwa was a separate, nominally superior position.
Eliminate option (c): Dewan is a revenue/administrative title from a different context (Mysore, Hyderabad, later princely states) — not the Maratha administrative designation for Nana's role.
Eliminate option (d): Senapati was the military commander role in the Maratha system — Nana Phadnavis was a civil-diplomatic figure, not a military commander.
Amatya was the title of the minister/administrator in the Maratha system — option (b) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits the common conflation of Nana Phadnavis with the Peshwa. In popular narrative, Nana is described as the 'power behind the throne' — but students who don't know his precise institutional title may assume he was himself the Peshwa. His title 'Amatya' (minister, specifically the revenue and diplomatic minister) is a specific institutional term in the Ashtapradhan (eight-minister) system of Shivaji — a cross-topic UPSC connection.
solution.final_explanation:
Nana Phadnavis was the de facto ruler of the Maratha Confederacy during the First Anglo-Maratha War period, but his institutional title was precise.

• Option (a) — Peshwa: Incorrect. The Peshwa was the prime minister/head of government, a separate and nominally superior position. During Nana's time, Sawai Madhavrao held the Peshwaship. Nana served under the Peshwa.
• Option (b) — Amatya: Correct. In the Maratha Ashtapradhan system, the Amatya was the finance and revenue minister. Nana Phadnavis held this position, which he used as the platform for his vast political influence.
• Option (c) — Dewan: Incorrect. Dewan was a title used in Mughal administration and later in Hyderabad and Mysore's bureaucratic structures — not the Maratha administrative title for Nana's role.
• Option (d) — Senapati: Incorrect. The Senapati was the military commander in the Ashtapradhan — a different portfolio entirely.

Value Addition:
• The Ashtapradhan (council of eight ministers) was established by Shivaji; Nana Phadnavis held the Amatya position within this framework.
• His full name was Balaji Janardan Bhanu; 'Phadnavis' referred to his administrative portfolio (keeper of accounts).
• Arthur Wellesley described Nana Phadnavis as 'the soul of the Maratha government' — a testament to his indispensability.

solution.concept_anchor: Baji Rao II — last Peshwa, not last Maratha ruler
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) states he was 'the last ruler of the Maratha Empire' — students who associate the abolition of the Peshwaship with the end of all Maratha power may choose this, without recognizing that other Maratha states (Gwalior, Indore, Nagpur) continued to exist as subsidiary states.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): Baji Rao II was not the Peshwa during the First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82) — that period involved Raghunathrao's claim and Sawai Madhavrao as the legitimate Peshwa. Baji Rao II became Peshwa much later.

Eliminate option (c): 'Last ruler of the Maratha Empire' is an overstatement — other Maratha states (Scindia of Gwalior, Holkar of Indore, Bhonsle of Nagpur, Gaikwad of Baroda) continued as subsidiary states after 1818.

Eliminate option (d): Baji Rao II attacked the British Residency at Khadki in 1817, not 1818 — and the characterization of this as a 'decisive military victory' is false; it was his attack that triggered the Third War and led to his defeat.
Option (a) correctly identifies him as the last Peshwa whose surrender in 1818 ended the institution of the Peshwaship — option (a) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c)'s scope-extension trap — 'last ruler of the Maratha Empire' — exploits the narrative of total Maratha collapse after 1818. While the Peshwaship was abolished, the Maratha Empire as a confederacy of five houses was not entirely extinguished — Scindia, Holkar, Bhonsle (though under subsidiary alliance), and Gaikwad continued as princely states. Baji Rao II was specifically the last Peshwa. The distinction between 'end of the Peshwaship' and 'end of all Maratha political existence' is precise and testable.
solution.final_explanation:
Baji Rao II's historical significance is precisely defined — and precision matters here.

• Option (a): Correct. Baji Rao II was the last Peshwa. After his surrender in 1818, the British formally abolished the Peshwaship, annexed Pune, and absorbed the Peshwa's territories into the Bombay Presidency. He was pensioned off at Bithur.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Baji Rao II was not Peshwa during the First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82). That period involved Raghunathrao's claim and, on the Pune side, Sawai Madhavrao as the legitimate Peshwa under Nana Phadnavis's guardianship.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Other Maratha states continued after 1818 — Gwalior (Scindia), Indore (Holkar), Nagpur (Bhonsle), and Baroda (Gaikwad) survived as subsidiary states until much later. Baji Rao II was not the last ruler of all Maratha states.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The Khadki attack was in 1817, not 1818, and it was not a 'decisive military victory' — it triggered British retaliation and led directly to Baji Rao II's ultimate defeat.

Value Addition:
• Baji Rao II died at Bithur in 1851; his adopted son Nana Saheb became a prominent leader of the 1857 uprising.
• The annexed Peshwa territories formed the core of the Bombay Presidency's Deccan districts.
• Gwalior (Scindia) and Baroda (Gaikwad) survived as princely states until 1947–48 — over 130 years after the Peshwaship's abolition.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) swaps Deogaon and Surji-Anjangaon between Bhonsle and Scindia — a plausible error since both treaties were signed in December 1803 and students may not remember which chief signed which.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Cuttack: Cuttack (Odisha) was ceded by Bhonsle under Deogaon — this geographic-chief connection is the strongest anchor; pair A-Deogaon with Bhonsle.
Delhi and Agra were Scindia's cessions — they correspond to Surji-Anjangaon; pair B-Surji-Anjangaon with Scindia.
Rajpurghat involved Holkar — the most resistant chief; pair C-Rajpurghat with Holkar.
The correct combination A-2, B-3, C-1 corresponds to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates between Bhonsle and Scindia — both had treaties in December 1803, making temporal clues useless. The geographic anchor (Cuttack = Bhonsle/Deogaon; Delhi/Agra = Scindia/Surji-Anjangaon) is the only reliable way to disambiguate. Students who do not associate Cuttack specifically with Bhonsle will swap the two treaties, landing on option (a). Rajpurghat's connection to Holkar is slightly more memorable because Holkar was the most resistant and his treaty was later (1806 finalization).
solution.final_explanation:
The three treaties ending the Second Anglo-Maratha War are a staple UPSC matching question — each must be paired precisely with its signatory Maratha chief.

Correct pairings:
• A (Treaty of Deogaon, 1803) → 2 (Bhonsle of Nagpur): Bhonsle ceded Cuttack (Odisha) and part of Berar. Cuttack gave the British the eastern coastal connection between Bengal and Madras.
• B (Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon, 1803) → 3 (Scindia): Scindia ceded Delhi, Agra, Broach, Ahmadnagar — and conceded British protectorate over the Mughal Emperor. Signed December 30, 1803.
• C (Treaty of Rajpurghat, 1803/1806) → 1 (Holkar): Holkar had the most complex resolution; the treaty terms were relatively favorable to him, and finalization extended to 1806 under Cornwallis's policy reversal.

Key trap: Students swap Deogaon and Surji-Anjangaon between Bhonsle and Scindia. The geographic anchor resolves this: Cuttack → Bhonsle (east India); Delhi/Agra → Scindia (north India).

Value Addition:
• Deogaon (December 17, 1803) was signed before Surji-Anjangaon (December 30, 1803) — Bhonsle submitted first.
• The Cuttack cession under Deogaon completed British coastal control from Bengal to Madras — a strategic masterstroke.
• Surji-Anjangaon made the British the protectors of the Mughal Emperor — a symbolic and political transformation of the highest order.

solution.concept_anchor: Salbai restored British prestige after Wadgaon humiliation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true and notice that diplomatic prestige was indeed restored after Wadgaon may quickly conclude R explains A without carefully examining whether R's specific content (status quo principle) is the cause of British prestige restoration.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — The Treaty of Salbai (1782) did restore British diplomatic standing after the humiliation of Wadgaon (1779) and the First War's inconclusive nature. A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Salbai did operate on a status quo ante principle: the British retained Salsette, Raghoba was pensioned off, and neither side made sweeping gains. R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — The status quo principle (R) is what Salbai implemented — and this very outcome, by ending the war without further British losses, did restore British prestige. R causally explains A: because Salbai reset the situation to broadly pre-war conditions (without British losing Salsette), British credibility as a regional power was restored.
Both A and R are correct and R explains A — correct option is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The Treaty of Salbai (1782) occupies a paradoxical place in British Indian history — it was neither a triumph nor a defeat, yet it marked a significant restoration of British strategic position after the disasters of Wadgaon and the First War's drift.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: After Wadgaon's humiliation (1779), where the Bombay army was forced to capitulate and sign away territories, Salbai provided a face-saving resolution. The British retained Salsette, received a 20-year peace, and saw their candidate (Madhavrao II) recognized as Peshwa.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Salbai was structured on a status quo ante principle — neither side made large territorial gains. The British did not press for punitive terms; the Marathas did not press their post-Wadgaon advantage.
• Causal relationship — R explains A: The status quo principle is precisely why British prestige was restored. By not suffering further territorial losses and securing a stable 20-year peace, the British demonstrated they remained a viable regional power despite the Wadgaon setback. The status quo outcome was the mechanism of prestige restoration.

Value Addition:
• The 20-year peace (1782–1803) gave the British time to consolidate in Bengal and South India before the Second War.
• Mahadji Scindia's mediation role at Salbai is often examined alongside his role as Mughal regent — two simultaneous power bases.
• Salbai is an example of how diplomatic outcomes can overshadow military results — the British were militarily weakened but diplomatically stabilized.
